utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to one and all. Case IT-04-74-T, Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I'd like to welcome all those present. In a few moments we're going to have the witness brought into the courtroom, and we shall be sitting today until 1.45. If nobody wishes to say anything, then we can have the witness shown in straight away. Yes, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Just briefly. We have received this morning from the Prosecution a document called "Prosecution's submission on the admission of documentary evidence." It appears to be making some legal submissions regarding the admissibility of the documents the Court was discussing yesterday. Your Honour, on reading this document, it would seem advisable for the Defence to consider making a written response, and accordingly we would ask the Trial Chamber to defer making a decision on the admissibility of those documents until we've had the opportunity to respond in writing. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. I appreciate Mr. Murphy's comments. Since it is the Prosecutor's submission, I would like to discuss it very briefly. The Prosecution, Your Honours, is very concerned with what appeared to be, and perhaps we misunderstood, but what appeared to be a ruling yesterday, or some statements yesterday on the admission of documentary evidence which, again with the greatest respect, we think are not only contrary to the prior guidelines and rulings made by this Trial Chamber, either the Pre-Trial Judge or the previous Trial Chamber or this Trial Chamber, but even more importantly, are inconsistent and contrary to the established jurisprudence and practice of this International Tribunal in establishing certain requirements for the admission of documentary evidence that are not the requirements, that are not the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and are contrary to the long-established practices in this Tribunal going back for many, many years. Of course, it's always a disadvantage for the Ad Litem Judges, for Judge Prandler, for Judge Trechsel, of course coming to the institution only a very few weeks ago and not to know what the long-established practices and customs of the institution are. We have provided a submission this morning to hopefully assist the Chamber in considering this issue further. To preview our final position, Your Honour, our position is that all of the ECMM documents should be admissible through this witness, that this witness can confirm the authenticity of every document. He has reviewed each document, can verify that these are official documents of the European Community Monitoring Mission. They are at that, they are what they purport to be, and that goes to authenticity. He can also, the documents on their face, establish their relevance. As we said in our submission, for most documents, for the vast majority of documents relevance can be determined or based upon the facial inspection of the document. Beyond those two requirements, some authentication: Is the document what it purports to be? Some threshold relevance. And the jurisprudence of the Tribunal is emphasise the word "some"; some relevance. Beyond those two things, Your Honour, the rest of these determinations all go to weight, and as the Trial Chamber has said repeatedly and as the Pre-Trial Judge has said repeatedly, the matter of weight is to be determined and given at the close of all of the evidence during the Trial Chamber's deliberations and the consideration of each piece of evidence, whether it be testimony or an exhibit, in the light of the overall trial record. And we submit, Your Honour, that that is the jurisprudence and practice of the Tribunal, and in many cases, and indeed I would -- I would say in virtually most cases, substantial amounts of documentary evidence has come into these trials without, without coming through or in connection with a particular witness. In many cases exhibits -- documents have been admitted from bar -- from counsel table based upon various representations by counsel, and that has been -- that has been a common practice in this Tribunal for years. So we invite the Chamber to reconsider its position, or perhaps if we misunderstood the statements yesterday, those can be clarified. We have made a filing today. It was filed with the Registry this morning, as Mr. Murphy has indicated, setting out what we believe the jurisprudence of the Tribunal to be. In a nutshell, Your Honour, and if the Court has again the courtesy copy that was distributed this morning, if I could direct the Court's and the courtroom's attention to page number 8. If I can just briefly indicate again. This, at the end of the day, in this 10-page submission is the summary, is the synopsis of the Prosecution position, and I'm sorry you didn't have those. I -- thank you. I'll give the Chamber a chance to look at that. And if you could please direct your attention to page 8. We believe, Your Honours, that the Tribunal jurisprudence and practice considers primarily three factors or considerations. First of all, as I've indicated a moment ago: Authenticity. Where did the document come from? Is it what it purports to be? In this case we have a witness -- we've got a witness on the witness stand who comes from ECMM, who by all indications, by all appearances, is a knowledgeable man, an educated man who has been very familiar with the record-keeping and reporting practices of ECMM. He has looked at every document, ECMM document the Prosecution wishes to tender, and based upon his familiarity with ECMM practices and record-keeping, he can say, and will say if he has not already, that all of these documents, however there may be - 360, something in that vicinity - that all of these documents are what they purport to be. They are all records and reports of the European Community Monitoring Mission. Now, secondly, again as we said a moment ago, is the document relevance -- is the document relevant? Excuse me. Does it bear some connection to the facts of this case? As we say here in our example, if the document on its face is about the expulsion of Muslim civilians in Stolac in July, August, 1993, then it is on its face relevant to the case. It bears on the facts of this case. And again, the jurisprudence is that it have "some relevance." Now, of course if one of us picks up a document and it's about something that happened in Tuzla in December, 1994, or about the World Cup in 2006, it's not relevant. The document is not relevant, or at least probably is not relevant based upon some very further showing that of course a party would have to make to show some connection, but generally presumptively, it would not be relevant unless some further linkage was made. Number 3, probative value or weight. Your Honour, again we submit that as this Trial Chamber and as this Pre-Trial Judge has said repeatedly, there is a very vast difference and distinction between admissibility and weight, and all these additional factors do indeed go to weight. And as we said about -- several lines into our point number 3 on page 9, the probative value or weight of a document should be determined in light of the overall evidence and positions and presentations of the parties in the case. If, at the end of the day, a document for a variety of reasons appears unreliable or appears substantially "out of sync" with the vast weight of the evidence, then the Chamber of course may accord it little or no value or weight at the end of the day. Your Honour, that's our submission. I have no problems, and indeed anticipated that the Defence may wish to make a written response. That would certainly be appropriate, we would certainly have no objection to that, but Your Honour, it's our fundamental position that these are the rules of evidence, and the admission of documentary evidence should apply in this case, and that this witness Mr. Beese can provide all necessary foundation for the admission of all of the ECMM exhibits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my only purpose in really addressing the matter today was to say that we would like the opportunity to consider this filing and respond to it. Unlike the Prosecution, we have every confidence in the abilities of Judge Prandler and Judge Trechsel to read and understand the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. We think that we can make it clear. The only point that I would make today in response to Mr. Scott's submission is there seems sometimes to be an assumption on the Prosecution's part that there are no rules of evidence at all at this Tribunal. In fact, Rule 89 makes it clear that the Chamber may only admit evidence which is relevant and which it deems to have probative value, and also that the Chamber may exclude evidence if that probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. So there is in fact a judicial function in scrutinising documents before they are admitted and it's not permissible for the Prosecution simply to present the Trial Chamber with a metre or two of documents and say we hereby move these in. Your Honour, that's all we're saying at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Regarding what was said, it is up to me to redefine matters. First of all, one must not forget that the proceedings underway -- in the proceedings underway, grosso modo, the Prosecution would like to show more than 9.000 documents, and this has never been seen in the experience of this Tribunal, that many documents. Secondly, if the Prosecution wishes to introduce about 9.000 documents, then the Defence would have the same right to introduce documents, which means that with this rhythm we would have 20.000 documents quite easily, which is something never seen by this Tribunal. It has never been confronted with anything like that. In your submissions that I was able to glance through over the past few minutes, you relate to three cases, Blaskic, Hadzihasanovic, and Simic. And in the Hadzihasanovic case, for example, I was the president of the Trial Chamber. In that particular trial we had 3.000 documents. Never in the history of this Tribunal did the Trial Chamber have that many documents. So I consider myself to be very well qualified to address the issue of documents. During the Status Conferences, we indicated several times - and this was confirmed by written rulings - that documents could -- must be introduced if and through a witness. That is a basic principle. And if we have a witness who is part of this European Mission, as in this case, the documents which he had knowledge of in exercising his duties within the European Mission should be presented to him. So documents he has knowledge of. Yesterday, I said that I noted in the pile of documents that I had here that there were documents which were dated posteriorly, that is to say which were compiled after the witness's departure, and I said that if the witness wasn't there any longer I don't see how this witness could say he could recognise or be asked to recognise a document which was compiled after he had left. And secondly, the second point was that during the testimony of the witness yesterday we found out that in May he wasn't there for 15 days, for a fortnight, so I assume that documents compiled during that period of time were documents which he did not see and have knowledge of, and so I indicated that today was the time to present him with these documents while he was exercising his function during his mission, and then he could say, yes, I know this document, I know that document, and so on and so forth. And then we would have the pertinent documents and of course the probative value and what weight we're going to attach to it would be determined later on. So it seems that you might not have understood all these reasons. So you put in a written submission, filed a written submission, and the Defence, quite legitimately, has the right to answer, to respond to your written submission, and then we're going to rule on the admission of documents. However, I'd like to point out at this juncture that in asking that these -- to -- that in filing a written submission, you might have a favourable or unfavourable ruling. That is at your own risk. So you're going to have to choose how you're going to introduce your evidence and exhibits, but in common law, the right of cross-examination, if documents have been admitted without allowing the Defence to cross-examine, they can in certain cases be a -- a problem for the future. Let me quote an example. Let me just quote an example. You have document 2612, for instance, which should not be presented to the witness, and you're asking for the admission of that document in a written submission. The document 2612, for instance, is a document, ECMM document, the 2nd of June, 1993, is the date, and the witness was certainly exercising his duties at that time, and it has to do with the capture of people -- of 100 persons by the HVO in May, 1993, who were taken to a detention centre; to Stolac, in fact. So that is a document which the Defence can cross-examine the witness on. And you are saying, no, we can have the document admitted by -- in written form. So that document can be presented to this witness in the coming few minutes, and he can say, "Yes, I confirm that such-and-such an event happened in Stolac." And then during the cross-examination at later stage, the Defence can examine the witness on that point. So I can do the same demonstration with other documents, using the example of other documents. I understand very well that the Defence wishes to introduce a maximum number of documents through -- in written form, or in writing, to gain time, because you have these 10.000 documents. So this intent on their part can impinge upon the Defence rights, because the Defence also has the right to examine. That is an absolute right. And so the Defence, having been apprised of your written submission will go through the documents one by one and the Judges will issue a final ruling. Perhaps we will support your proposal, perhaps we will reject it. We'll see in due course, having given it due thought. But for the moment, the course to take is when you have a witness here, you should present him with the documents that he drafted himself or documents that he had knowledge of. I don't think you understood this, but that's your problem. And let me remind you that in the interests of justice, the Judges should be in possession of all the elements, all the pertinent elements, and then those elements will be the subject of a debate, because how else can we, when faced with thousands of exhibits, thousands of documents, not ask useful questions on important documents? So you have to sift through the documents, decide which you're going to present, which you're not going to present, and then you're going to ask to have them tendered into evidence. Maybe my colleagues would like to intervene at this point, and I give them the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a request from one of the parties before us. The other party will have the right to comment. Then we, the Chamber, will discuss it. I think it is not conducive to the good exercise of our task if these matters, now the substance is discussed before we have even had time to read the request let alone the answer of the Defence. We will not interrupt, I think, to decide this immediately. We will sit this afternoon. I would suggest that the Prosecution goes through the motions they think are necessary to make these documents admissible, and then we will hear comments from the Defence, and I think then we in Chamber will deliberate and come to a conclusion. That's the proceeding -- the way to proceed that I would propose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Defence like to address the matter? Counsel Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. I totally agree with Judge Trechsel, even though yesterday we parted ways on certain objections. I thought it was perhaps premature for Mr. Scott to go ahead and give an oral presentation of this -- of his -- of his submission. We would like a chance just to respond. I would also suggest to the Prosecution that they do whatever they feel is necessary today. We will not be objecting for the sake of objecting. If we feel that it is necessary for us to state a position, we will state a position. It will be probably a position that is joint. We don't -- we don't want to obstruct, and so I do think it would be appropriate, particularly given some confusion that after you hear submissions, oral submissions on the documents being presented today, that you deliberate on it. But for future purposes, we do need an opportunity to thoroughly review this and compose a joint response which we believe would more or less tailor what Professor Murphy has indicated on the record. And I might add that one of his specialties is evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judge would like to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I simply would like to say at this juncture that I share the views expressed by my fellow Judge, Judge Trechsel, and I really feel that after the presentation of the Prosecutor's views on that issue, and also after we have heard both Mr. Murphy and Mr. Karnavas then we are going to consider the matter again and then we have to come to a conclusion. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I -- one minute. Thank you, Your Honour, one minute. Of course, as I said, we fully anticipated in making a written submission that the Defence would make the appropriate responses in the time -- whatever time the Court provides. That was a given, of course. And of course if the Chamber wishes to make a written ruling, that also is of course expected, and of course we know that the Chamber might rule for us, they might rule against us. That is the nature of the exercise. Your Honour, since this has come up repeatedly, I do want to make one statement, not only about the documents but the case in general. I want to be very clear on this: The Prosecution makes no apology for the size or complexity of this case. It is what it is. Perhaps in the future when war criminals are committing crimes, they will consider smaller, simpler crimes. I will today ask, and hopefully this will be broadcast, to all future war criminals, please commit only simple, easy-to-prove crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object. I object to those comments, Mr. President. I think they're totally inappropriate. To be referring to the accused as war criminals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Karnavas, you'll have the floor in a moment. Allow Mr. Scott to finish and then you can speak after him. If you keep interrupting and intervening, we'll get nowhere. So I want each of the parties to be able to present their views, and your time will come to present your views and to respond to what Mr. Scott has said. Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my comment just now was not directed to these accused specifically but to the principles in general, and if you look at the transcript on page 12, you will see that. I'm quite familiar, Your Honours -- well, let me just finish that thought. We will present -- Your Honour, the Prosecution is doing its very best, has done its very best, will continue to do its very best to present indeed a complex, large, and difficult case to you as best we can, and undoubtedly we will make mistakes and undoubtedly it will not be a perfect case, but I can assure the Chamber that this is a large, important case and we will do our very best to present it to you as best we can. As to the practice of common law cross-examination, Your Honour, I can assure the Chamber I -- I, too, like Mr. Karnavas and like Mr. Murphy, have been doing this, have been practising common law cross-examination for at least the past 27 years and I, too, like many other people in the courtroom, have routinely caught -- taught trial advocacy in the common law system. So no one needs to remind us of their credentials on this. I think everyone in the courtroom can be presumed to be a professional in this regard. Our position on the documents has nothing to do with the cross-examination. It is the admission of the documents themselves. Of course, of course the Defence has every right to conduct a full cross-examination within the bounds of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, including as to Mr. Beese, and I am quite confident, I'm quite confident that the cross-examination of Mr. Beese will be an extensive and complete one. Finally, Your Honour, I will just indicate, and again, I fully agree that the matter should be briefed, but I just want to look ahead. If the Trial Chamber -- if the guideline remains as indicated yesterday, then the Prosecution, with all respect, asks the Trial Chamber, all three Judges of the Trial Chamber, to then give us very clear -- a very clear ruling as to what additional piece of evidence is required from a particular witness to establish the necessary foundation for the admission of a document beyond what we have said this morning. If there is something more the Chamber wants, if there's some additional piece of evidence the Chamber says is necessary, we need to know this, because we have a long trial ahead of us, we indeed have hundreds and thousands of exhibits, and if those rules are not very, very clear and we can prepare our case and find our witnesses and present our case as best we can, it's very, very difficult. So if there is some additional piece of evidence, beyond authenticity, beyond what the document purports to be, beyond being relevant on its face, we need the Chamber to tell us very, very clearly what that additional item is. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It is my habit, and perhaps it's a bad habit, to interrupt when I hear offensive comments coming from the Prosecution, and I have no -- I make no apologies for interrupting a Prosecutor when I feel he or she is offending my client or other accused in the court. I thought Mr. Scott's comments, though he claims were not directed to these accused, were nonetheless inappropriate, not just for this Tribunal but in any court to make those suggestions. And secondly, I would like to say that it is the Prosecutor that chose to draft the indictment in the way he did. It's regrettable that this Tribunal has had a practice of rubber stamping, more or less, the previous indictments and perhaps not being more attentive at the beginning in requiring a proofing chart as this Trial Chamber had requested. I know that measures are being taken now to rectify those -- those issues, but nonetheless, the Prosecutor chose a very wide indictment with a lot of documents, many of them which are not necessarily relevant, and I think it is the responsibility of the Prosecutor to establish relevancy. I don't want to go into the merits of this. I merely interrupted, however, because I thought Mr. Scott was beyond the pale with his comments, and I think he owes the accused in this courtroom an apology. That's what I think. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just briefly. I would like to follow on from what my colleague Mr. Karnavas just said in launching protests about what the Prosecutor said. I have a concrete solution. I propose that we delete from the record the statement made by the Prosecutor in line -- on page 12, line 11, because the presumption of innocence is a principle which functions in all courts and must function here, because he categorically stated that we -- here we have war criminals. A judgement has not yet been made. We don't know about that, and I think there is no place for things like that in the record. So I'd like to have this redacted from the record. Page 12, the sentence begins on line 11. Because the implications are quite clear, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to deliberate this afternoon with respect to the redaction of page 12, line 11, from the record. I have understood that the Defence would like to respond in writing to the admissibility motion, as Mr. Murphy stated a moment ago. So we can give a ruling either in oral form or written form once we have both sides' written responses. So we're going to make a ruling at the beginning of next week, once we have all your written responses. Very well. We conferred straight away on the expungence, on the redaction of the transcript. As far as line 11 is concerned, that is a hypothesis, "... and perhaps in the future, if war criminals ..." So those are hypotheses; if. And we can't say that hypotheses in the future can be applied to the present, so there's no call for the Trial Chamber to order that portion redacted and expunged, because the phrase and sentence applied to the future, envisaging other persons. And Mr. Scott, in continuation, explained that he did not have in mind the persons present in this courtroom. So there is no need to redact that. Now, with respect to the written decision, the written ruling on the admissibility of exhibits and evidence, we are going to do that once we've received your written submissions and have studied them. So as soon as possible send in your written submissions, and joint ones as you did in the previous cases of appeal, and then we'll study them straight away. Having said that and having spent half an hour discussing that point, we're now going to have the witness shown in, and of course the Prosecution is free to present any documents it likes to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. The Chamber took a few moments before we had you introduced because we had a matter to attend to beforehand. As the problem is on the road to being resolved, without further ado, I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution to carry on the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Beese.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yesterday when we broke we were discussing meetings that you had had involving Mr. Stojic. Based on your meetings with him, sir, did you on any occasion make any observations concerning his authority?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to object, but once again may it be made clear as to whether the witness is now going to testify from his personal knowledge, which would be acceptable, or whether he is going to speculate and give an opinion on this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, the question was: "Based on your meetings with him, did you on any occasion make any observations concerning his authority?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, I would ask you to carefully consider that question as put to you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic appeared to have full authority. His subordinates certainly deferred to him with considerable respect, and I never had reason to believe in my dealings across the region that his authority was questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, what is the basis for your statement that Mr. Stojic appeared to have full authority?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were occasions in the field, particularly during cease-fire talks and disengagements, where if we came across resistance from more junior HVO commanders, at some point we would not be able to take matters further and would notify the junior commander that we were referring the matter to his superiors in Mostar, and particularly Mr. Stojic, at which point the demeanour of the junior officer usually changed and became more cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Beese, can you point to any particular instances where this was the case? You've mentioned occasions in the field. Can you give us any particular examples?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were occasions in the Gornji Vakuf cease-fire talks, both with Zeljko Siljeg prior to the cease-fire and then later to junior commanders in Pajic Polje, where we thought it necessary to remind them of the commitments given by their superiors, and that is not specifically Mr. Stojic, that is the superiors in Mostar, meaning Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, or General Petkovic, and on those occasions both the gentlemen concerned became a great deal more cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I believe you testified about this yesterday, but could you tell us who Mr. Stojic's deputy was?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it was Mr. Slobodan Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your meetings, can you tell us or describe for us the relationship between Mr. Stojic and Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic -- Mr. Bozic was appointed the interface between the Ministry of Defence and international agencies. Therefore, while initially we spoke directly with Mr. Stojic - that is myself, Ray Lane, and others - in the latter months if we had a concern and addressed it to the ministry, we would address it directly to Mr. Bozic who would receive our concerns, assist us where he could, or refer the matter to his superiors, which in all cases would be Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, you just mentioned "if we had a concern." What type of concern or concerns did you convey to the HVO Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had concerns for access. If we wished to move to an area, as I've earlier said, to Stolac, for instance, we would have to gain a pass from the Ministry of Defence, in which case we would obtain it through Mr. Bozic. But if we had concerns about denial of access that had previously been agreed, such as access to Doljani and Sovici, we would apply to the Ministry of Defence through Mr. Bozic for access again and remind him of the commitments of his party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the result of these instances where you expressed concern for access to these areas after having raised them with Mr. Bozic or the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On occasion access might be improved. Perhaps it depended upon our own demeanour and how -- how we presented our case, whether forcefully or less forcefully, although Mr. Bozic was usually concerned to hear that we were frustrated, and committed to attend to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what steps were taken by Mr. Bozic to attend to the matter?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of access to areas that were denied, it usually made no difference at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I'd now like to turn your attention to Mr. Petkovic. You testified yesterday that you met with him on a number of occasions. Can you tell us approximately how many occasions you met with Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall specifically, I'm afraid, but it would have been quite regularly during certain periods of my stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can -- I can say it was more than 20, less than 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the subject matters of the discussion with Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were usually concerned with cease-fire arrangements where a cease-fire was to be brokered or implemented. Then we were dealing with General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And based on these meetings, sir, can you tell us anything about Mr. -- or General Petkovic's demeanour?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my meetings with Mr. Petkovic and observing him through those meetings, whether the meetings were chaired by me or simply observed by me, he was a very calm man in discussion, forceful, persistent, but not the least bit impolite to anyone, whether it was those of us internationally or his apparent adversaries. The only matter I have cause to question on is that, given the number of cease-fires that he attended and brokered and that were immediately broken, one has to question the sincerity of some of his actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, can you gives any examples of these cease-fires you just described?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have related a number in my account, but most specifically in Gornji Vakuf, later agreements in Medjugorje, Mostar, Vitez, and -- and a number more that I was not attending to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than these cease-fire discussions, do you recall any other topics that you discussed with General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, if you were able, based on these meetings that you had with General Petkovic, to have any observations concerning his relationship either upwards or downwards with the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my experience, his subordinates, that is junior military commanders, deferred to him and always gave him the floor to speak. He was evidently the senior person present in cease-fire talks where he was present. He himself deferred to Mostar. He appeared to know exactly what was required of him by his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, when you mentioned on line 14 junior military commanders, can you tell us, if you recall, any specific junior military commanders you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, and Colonel Miroslav Lasic. I can also say I think that Colonel Tihomir Blaskic was -- was a subordinate of -- of similar level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate, sir, upon the statement you made on line 17 and 18, "He appeared to know exactly what was required of him by his superiors." What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that a cease-fire would usually follow political direction from Mostar, his responsibility was to implement a cease-fire. He appeared to know whether he needed to hurry through that cease-fire, agree it and implement it, or delay it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you personally aware, Mr. Beese, of any situations where it appeared to you that General Petkovic did not exercise effective control over his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only case I witnessed was the case that I referred to in the Dario Kordic trial, but that was dealing with a politician rather than a military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I'd now like to turn your attention to Mr. Coric. You mentioned him yesterday. Do you recall approximately how many times you met with Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe no more than about five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the time period when you had those meetings?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early -- in the mid-part of my tour; that is, February, March and April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, what were the reasons that you went to see Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked to speak to him on the matters of the abductees in Mostar, the abductees of the night of the 5th of February, to see if the HVO had completed their investigation and were prepared to release a report. I also raised with him the matter of the transportation of prisoners by ambulance, which we witnessed in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did these meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with Mr. Coric in an office in the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate in any way upon this issue of the matter of the transportation of prisoners by ambulance?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was personally concerned to see what appeared to me the routine carriage of prisoners in ambulances, that is people who were dressed in uniform but were not armed, were not badged, and appeared to be prisoners of the armija, travelling through Mostar in the backs of ambulances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you went to see Mr. Coric, Mr. Beese, what capacity was he serving in?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the Vojna Policija, the HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your observations as an ECMM monitor, what were the functions of the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: While they were military police, and while it is not unusual in conflict to find that military police have greater powers than in peacetime, it did appear that the Vojna Policija carried out the direction of both political and military government in Mostar and therefore they were not simply confined to military matters. If something had to be done in policing terms, for better or worse, it was usually carried out generally by the Vojna Policija as opposed to routine traffic issues and such like carried out by the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, before it disappears off the screen, I just would like to ask a question of clarification concerning the prisoners that were in the ambulance. What -- of what military force were the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were from the armija, from their uniforms and their demeanour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What force was holding those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Beese, based on your meetings with Mr. Coric, can you convey any observations concerning his demeanour?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke very good English. He was very straightforward to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn your attention, Mr. Beese, to a subject that we touched on briefly yesterday, and that's the hierarchy with respect to command and control within the HVO. Can you please describe for us who was at the top of the HVO chain of command.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comments will be based on my observations only. I was not a student of the structure of the HDZ or the HVO and therefore my observations were purely based on practical experience and expediency at the time. It was quite apparent to me, most particularly when I met Mate Boban on the 8th of May, that he was the senior figure in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the Bosnian Croats. On that particular day, others in the meeting, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Zubak, Mr. Bozic, Mr. Stojic, deferred to Mr. Boban. Mr. Boban had a forceful character, a sharp eye, and a sharp mind. He appeared to be the senior party. The next senior party appeared to be Mr. Jadranko Prlic, who, as I've said before, appeared to know all things and appeared to be able to give direction on all matters, whether civilian or military. Mr. Stojic was evidently senior in the military hierarchy. I would have assumed him to be the commander of military forces, albeit through generals. Those were -- were the principal senior players that I dealt with. There were a number of more junior ministers, including Mr. Coric running the military police, Mr. Tadic running humanitarian affairs, and the mayors of a number of towns who, like Jozo Maric, was not only a mayor, I understand of Grude, but also responsible for matters of culture and education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I neglected to ask you this earlier, but on those occasions when you met with Mr. Stojic, what type of clothing was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a few moments ago based on your observations that you were -- or that your comments are based on observations and that you're not a student, and you indicated the HDZ. "I'm not a student of the structure of the HDZ." Based upon your observations, can you tell us what the HDZ was?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it to be the political party from which the HVO was descended. There are -- it is quite possible to attach a badge, a name to anything. Ultimately it was my responsibility to determine who was responsible and for what. It didn't particularly matter what they called themselves, referred to themselves as, or what badge they carried, and therefore whether something was referred to as an HDZ policy or an HVO policy or a Croat policy, to me it was one and the same. We are talking here about a nationalist movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, in terms of your dealings with HVO military officials, did anyone ever raise with you the issue of uncontrolled elements or irregular militia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we had cause to complain that certain activities were taking place, whether it was the attacks on villages, burning of villages, even shelling around Gornji Vakuf, I was frequently deflected with comments about uncontrolled elements or irregulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What steps as an ECMM monitor did you take to investigate these claims or to verify these claims?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not always possible to gain access to areas in which elements operated, whether regular or irregular. Therefore, we noted the claim that a particular action was carried out by a -- an unaccountable or irregular force, and we could do little more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular incidents where this issue arose?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were claims of uncontrolled elements working for both parties. There were uncontrolled elements said to be working around Doljani and Pasovici, clearing Muslim villages, but there were counterclaims from the HVO of uncontrolled or extreme elements operating in Central Bosnia also for the Moslem party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to focus your attention on these claims of uncontrolled elements in Doljani and Pasovici. Do you recall any of the specific discussions that you had as an ECMM monitor concerning those claims?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expressed concern for -- for the advances and activities in Sovici and Doljani as I knew of them, but as I couldn't see them and couldn't identify the persons at the time, it was difficult for me to -- to carry the matter further. Reports from monitors from those areas did report that when they attempted to enter the area of Doljani and Sovici they were turned back by people who did not appear to be regular HVO. They appeared to be irregulars with a separate agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, did you raise this issue with any HVO commanders on the ground?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concern at the time was more for the granting of access so we could prove matters for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now to another topic that was again raised yesterday on several occasions. You indicated confrontation between the Serbs and the HVO and the ABiH forces.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, based on your time as an ECMM monitor and your observations on the ground, were you able to observe relations between the HVO and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Murphy -- Mr. Mundis. I don't even see you. Might I return to this access and irregular forces issue. Have I understood correctly that there were instances when the HVO authorities had granted a right to access to Doljani and Sovici and then monitors were stopped by personnel which was not regular HVO personnel? Is that what you were telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, on a number of occasions we complained to the HVO authorities that will we had not gained access to the Doljani-Sovici area when access had been granted by the authorities in Mostar. We explained that a number of teams had been turned back by -- by Croat personnel who we could not necessarily identify as HVO though it was remarked to me by monitors that when they encountered these people, they did not appear to be a formal military formation, they appeared to be irregulars or some such. They had very little discipline. In fact, a German monitor, Klaus Nissen, was turned back from a checkpoint with a Nazi salute and a recommendation that he return to his country of origin. When we complained about these matters, we understood that it would be very simple for the HVO leadership to communicate with their people in the area. They had direct access by road through Tomislavgrad. There was no obstruction to them. There were known to be significant numbers of HVO forces and HV forces in that area. There's no reason why access would not have been granted nor authority exercised over these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, just staying on the subject of irregular or -- irregular forces or uncontrolled elements, did you ever -- on any occasion did you ever personally observe uncontrolled elements or irregular forces engaged in combat?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The behaviour of people in conflict and their appearance did not necessarily demonstrate their membership of any particular structure, regular or irregular. At times of conflict, uniforms become worn, grubby, badging less distinct, appearance less distinct. It is not always possible to determine whether someone's a regular or an irregular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me now return to the subject that I was about to go to, and that is relations between the HVO and the Serbs. Did you as part of your duties on any occasion observe situations of cooperation between those forces?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please elaborate or explain those instances to us.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- there were two -- two distinctly different interests here. The first was a wish expressed to me by Jozo Maric that he be able to visit Banja Luka and to have detailed discussion with the Serbs there. He alluded to matters of prisoner exchange and to other bilateral relations. That was in -- in March, 2003 [sic]. Then again, a little later, there were discussions between Mr. Maric and, I believe, Colonel Milosevic, the Serb commander of the Trebinje area, on matters of mutual interest. That is one side, the desire to have improved communications with them. Our teams did monitor and witness a degree of cooperation between the Croats and the Serbs in so much as when Travnik was attacked by the HVO on the 4th of June, I believe it was, and the HVO forces, forced to withdraw from that area, they passed west through the Serb lines, south-west through Serb territory and back into Herzegovina in the south. The same thing happened when the HVO ceased to cooperate with the armija in Zepce later in the year. The -- there was evidently a degree of collusion where Serb armour was brought in from the front line to support a Croat attack on Zepce. The Croats later withdrew west through the front lines in that area and back again down through Herzegovina. The same happened in the Konjic area where the Croat citizens --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the record, page 29, line 8, it says that it was a meeting in March, 2003. So that's obviously a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. 1993. To return to my answer: Croatian people were withdrawn from the Konjic area also through the Serb lines to the east and back south again into Herzegovina. I believe that demonstrates a degree of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, just for the record, when we -- when you refer to Serb forces, what -- of what military force were these Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you happen to know its abbreviation in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have referred to it as the BSA, but, no, I have no further knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, because on page 28, line 10, you made reference to HV forces in the area in response to an earlier question. Can you elaborate upon that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll just go -- just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This part of your answer -- I'll just read the sentence two sentences prior to this. This is on line 8 through 10 on page 28: "They had direct access by road through Tomislavgrad. There was no obstructions to them. There were known to be significant numbers of HVO forces and HV forces in that area."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is area south-west between Prozor and Tomislavgrad and west of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the basis for your conclusion or your testimony that there were HV forces in that area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our monitors had reported the presence of HV forces for a number of weeks in that area. I personally saw HV forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate time period that you saw HV forces in that area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Late February through March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the number of occasions. I can think of at least two occasions when I personally saw HV personnel and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know they were HV personnel and trucks?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion I saw HV plates on the back of a truck. That's registration plates, badging. More generally, if one saw significant numbers of troops -- and by "significant numbers," on one occasion our monitors reported the movement of 30 buses full of troops from Split through Tomislavgrad to the north. The troops frequently disembarked in Tomislavgrad. They wore new uniforms, they were freshly cut, dressed, and not at all of an irregular bearing. They didn't appear to be experienced, they had the nervous swagger of new soldiers, new to an area, and on some occasions through Herzegovina one saw troops with HVO badges pinned to their arms rather than sewn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why would the troops one saw in Herzegovina have HVO badges pinned to their arms rather than sewn?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days there was a denial of the presence of HV forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, you mentioned that you saw these people in the area south-west of Prozor and Tomislavgrad and west of Jablanica. Did you see them in any other locations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reports of them in Southern Herzegovina, around Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, did you personally prepare any reports on HV involvement in the conflict during the time that you were there as an ECMM monitor?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when you made such reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report would have been written around the time that I moved from the south to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P 02620.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see a document before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a report submitted by me to the ECMM office in Zagreb concerning HV involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, how do you know that this document was submitted by yourself?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it is shown at the top to be from the Deputy Head of Mission, RC Zenica. That would have been me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you go down, please -- if we could go down to paragraph 2 of this -- or section 2 of this document. Does this section, Mr. Beese, set forth your observations concerning HV support?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if you note section 3, which begins on the bottom of this page and continues on the next page, can you tell us what that is, please? Go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, this part of the report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a -- as much evidence as we could summon on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Beese, concerning this report, who actually drafted it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did you base this report on? What was the source of information contained in this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personal observations of HV forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the considerable reports in writing from my teams, and personal recount from my teams. There were, of course, many claims from the armija of such. Sometimes the claims were exaggerated. In this particular case it was essential that we proved it for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than this report, Mr. Beese, that you yourself drafted, were you aware of any other ECMM reports concerning HV involvement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may ask a question with regard to this document. When one looks at the top of it, it has again a date and mentions which clearly are procedural and related to the OTP. Is this an original document where this heading was added or is it a document that was copied from another document, retyped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the original report that I wrote was written without the various headings, times, and the like. It is -- it is possible that it was copied onto a Capsat machine from a report of mine. I did produce the original report on Capsat. It was the only means we had to type. We had to type through a Capsat machine. It may well have been stored on one of the very few personal computers we had in Zenica and then cut and pasted onto a Capsat machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you be a bit more precise perhaps as to how much editing has been done. You have told us that the headlines have been added. Has there been other editing done to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not getting any interpretation. I will repeat my question. I am addressing Mr. Mundis. Looking at this document, P 02620, initially it was a part of other documents, and now I am asking you whether this document should be under seal or not, because when we were first discussing some documents under Rule 70, you asked that they be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I can -- I can certainly address that issue of -- that Your Honour has expressed. Some -- perhaps I could go into private session, please, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So in open session, I would like to say that we referred to document P 02620, an ECMM document that was presented to the witness. So we're going to continue with the examination-in-chief after the break, because it's 10.30, and we'll reconvene at ten minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, right before the break we were discussing your 3 June -- or 3 June, 1993, report on HV involvement. Were you aware if at any time after your report was drafted whether an update report was prepared?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I initially prepared a report whilst working in Southern Herzegovina. A second version was produced at the request of Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault for presentation to headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When was that report prepared or produced?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second report, I believe the one we're looking at, on the 3rd of June is the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After your report was prepared, do you know of an update to your 3 June, 1993, report was produced?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Jean-Pierre Thebault referred to it and possibly added further information in his own reports later but it was not replaced as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you have any knowledge as to when Ambassador Thebault added further information in his own reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you become aware that Ambassador Thebault may have added to your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sight of reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask, Mr. President, that the witness be shown P 03827. I do note for the record as of yet we -- we do have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, do you see a document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What -- what is this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an update on the involvement of the -- HV involvement in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say it's an update, an update of what?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to my previous report. It is presumably an update to that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who drafted this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was produced by Jean-Pierre Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is announced at the top that it's from the head of the regional centre Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beese. I'd now like to turn to a topic again that was discussed yesterday, and that was humanitarian convoys. During the time, sir, that you were with the ECMM, do you know if any reports were produced concerning restrictions on humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The various teams working on convoy routes, such as mine initially in the Mostar area, would have referred the matter of convoy restrictions to the headquarters in Split and Zenica. The headquarters in Zenica would refer the matter to Zagreb, and I believe there were special reports written by the humanitarian office of the ECMM in Zagreb about these affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Beese, how would these headquarters have produced reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally using information received by the teams in theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the specific dates of any such reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown P 02424.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see that document, Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, based on the face of this document, what it is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document written by Christian Warming, a political analyst in the headquarters Zagreb, based on reports given him from the regional centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we please go to the second page of this document. And who produced this document, Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is from the head of regional centre, Jean-Pierre Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the subject of this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerns the freedom of movement on roads necessary for humanitarian transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, if we could please go back to the top of that, or if you could focus your attention on the top of this document. Do you have any knowledge about the information contained at the top of this document above the line that says "From"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the line at that starts "NL Burum ..." which refers to the particular satellite system through which this message was transmitted, the message was transmitted apparently on the 16th of May, and it gives the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you -- do you know what those square stamps on the right-hand side indicate?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with them. Those would appear to be the stamps of receipt and transmission by the communications centre in the Hotel I, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown P 03627.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see that document, Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a further report on the roads and transportation of humanitarian aid, sent by the head of regional centre Zenica, Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault, to the headquarters of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again the line above the line that says "From HRC Zenica," what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you can just draw the document to the top. That again is the transmission methodology; sent by Capsat on the 23rd of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us now -- turning to another topic, Mr. Beese. Can you tell us about any instructions that ECMM received concerning -- again in late May. I want to focus your attention on late May, early June, 1993. To your knowledge, did ECMM receive any instructions concerning the implementation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what those instructions were?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was agreement between the HVO and Presidency that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan should be implemented as far as it could in free Bosnia, and the ECMM was instructed by the Zagreb headquarters to assist with the implementation of that peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the specifics as to what ECMM was to do with respect to the implementation of this plan?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: ECMM was to ensure as best it could that all parts of free Bosnia understood that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was to be implemented and to give guidance to local authorities as to how they might proceed to prepare for implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what type of guidance was to be given to local authorities as to how they might proceed to prepare for implementation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a need, first of all, to convince local authorities that this was a genuine request, given that the area was far from quiet and peaceful. Secondly, to ensure that they had time to nominate their representatives region by region, party by party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there issues concerning whether this request was genuine? Because you've told us you needed to convince local authorities that this was a genuine request. Why was that necessary?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many local officials could hardly believe that, given the degree of hostility and unrest in the region, that it was at all feasible to implement a normal -- a normal civil institution. They believed it to be impossible. So, to an extent, did we.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why? Why did you believe it to be impossible?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two principal concerns: The first was that it wasn't -- it wasn't feasible for the parties to prepare for implementation. I was aware that delegates in Central Bosnia, while travelling to and from towns through front lines in the course of their business, had been either brutalised or, in some cases, killed. That meant that some parties would be disinclined to put forward their best men if they were going to be either imprisoned or killed. Secondly, the Vance-Owen Plan at that stage, with its description of provinces 8 and 10, were still taken by the HVO to mean that they would run that not simply as an area for which they were responsible but for which they had total control and ownership of despite the fact that in many parts of it they did not hold majority by population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Beese, that this was "... still taken by the HVO to mean ..." can you tell us who you were referring to within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Discussions with Mr. Prlic in Mostar had given us cause for concern, but he gave us reason to believe that if the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was implemented, that they would have total control and therefore they would impose their choice of culture, education on the -- on the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just as a point of clarification since my client is mentioned, and I know I do get to cross-examine, but he's mentioning "us," and I would like to know, perhaps Mr. Mundis, this is his next question, whether he's going to tell us whether this is firsthand knowledge or hearsay; and if it's hearsay, from whom. That way I could better prepare for my cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, sir? When you said "he gave us reason to believe," were you personally in attendance at meetings where this was discussed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I refer to a meeting with Mr. Prlic that is described in my account.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where we might find that in your account, or the date?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In meetings leading up to the Mostar meeting of 18 April. Therefore, between the 1st and the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the witness's account as marked yesterday, I believe that might still be with the registrar or the usher, if that could be provided to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask, Mr. Beese, if you could please leaf through that until you find the appropriate passage or passages.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no apparent reference to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and our concerns during the meetings, and I'm referring to particularly, I think, to the meeting of 15 or 16 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Beese, if you could turn your attention back to paragraph 296, which is on page 56, and perhaps looking at the preceding page where a date is indicated.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 296 reflects meetings held on what day, or a meeting held on what day?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indicates here the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who was in attendance at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jean-Pierre Thebault, myself, and Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please read paragraph 296 out loud.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It was always difficult to listen with patience to such political dogma. Prlic had a new agenda which bore no resemblance to my own proposal for the setting up of joint municipal commissions. On the contrary. The Vance-Owen Plan suggested to the HVO that they would in principle control Herzegovina and Central Bosnia right up to the line between Travnik and Kiseljak. The Lasva Valley. And the HVO thought that they would own this patch. They never questioned the difference between having responsibility for an area and outright ownership of a province. Prlic wanted his schools to teach the Croatian language and customs. He wanted the HVO car registration plate system to predominate and for the BiH forces in HVO provinces to disband completely or to surrender to HVO control. Nothing, not one tiny element in the discussion suggested room for negotiation or for compromise."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Beese, what was the basis for you writing this paragraph in your account?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my conclusion drawn from the conversations of the meeting with Mr. Prlic and Ambassador Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: A meeting at which you attended.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you if you can elaborate upon that portion of the report where you indicated a difference between having responsibility for an area and outright ownership of a province. Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The production of maps for the Vance-Owen Plan had on occasion been coloured to show who had responsibility for them and were produced presumably to demonstrate to each of the three parties to the plan that there was an element of fairness or sharing out of responsibility by territory. However, that's a very different thing to the way by which you run an area for which you are responsible, and consistent with the lack of evidence of any consultation with or discussion with the Muslim or Bosnian faction, it was apparent that the HVO gave direction not through discussion but achieved their aims through direction and control. That is not a normal way to bring a minority, or even a majority in some areas, to your thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One other point of clarification: Might we know what his proposal was and where we can find it? Because he notes that "my own --" "it did not --" "which bore no resemblance to my own proposal." This is in paragraph 296. I assume that he had a proposal, he myself; he had such authority. And of course I would suspect that he had a proposal in writing or one was memorialised someplace. If we could get some answers regarding this particular point. I think it's very vital to our discussion today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And of course -- and of course it can be covered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That didn't -- I was aware of that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of course, I'm sure this will also be explored in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Beese, can you tell us about the reference in paragraph 296 to what appears to be your own proposal for setting up joint municipal commissions.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had been a consistent theme in the context of cooperation and a reduction of tension that in each town a conference be established or a commission where both parties were present. Given the level of tension in the area and conflict, if those commissions, conferences, could not regularly meet and resolve their disputes, it would be impossible to implement a political solution to open conflict, and therefore I had proposed that a prerequisite to the implementation of any plan every town should have a commission with two parties sitting at the table full time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, how was your proposal to establish these commissions conveyed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My proposal dates back much earlier and is consistent with our need to bring parties together to end conflict, not solely to implement a political solution. There was a need for both parties to be at the table all the time and not simply when the international agencies suggested that for once they should talk to each other over a table. So it was not produced solely as a solution to implementation of the Vance Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was your proposal set forth in a document or orally at meetings or both or in some other manner?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At meetings I would have suggested on every occasion that it was necessary for the two parties to talk and work together, so therefore is not set down as a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me now turn to another topic that was mentioned briefly yesterday, being the concept of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to ask with respect to paragraph 296. You said that you proposed to Mr. Prlic to create a commission in -- a mixed commission in the municipality. Now, was that an initiative that you took yourself? Was it a idea that came from you, or were you exercising what was decided on the basis of the Vance-Owen Plan?
