So was it your own initiative or were you transmitting to Mr. Prlic what should be implemented within the frameworks of the implementation of the overall Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we received very little direction from our superiors in Zagreb as to how we were going -- we were to go about this task. We in RC Zenica discussed it amongst ourselves, the senior monitors, as to how this could be implemented given the conditions. It would have been a prerequisite, I think, under anybody's understanding of the implementation of a political solution that there should be some means by which the two parties would come together in every municipality. They did not because of the conflict. It was a concept that we believed was essential for success of the plan. It was not a plan given to us by our superiors in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That was a very precise answer. Now, with respect to this municipal commission, did you personally speak to people from the municipalities in Mostar, for instance, and say that they should take part in the work of these mixed commissions? Because we have the impression that your contacts were only with certain persons from the HVO. Did you contact other persons in the municipality, in the field? Did you have any other contacts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our teams spoke with the heads of municipalities and the authorities of both sides across the region, but for us, if you like, centrally, that's the head of regional centre and myself, the principal concern was that delegates, for instance, from the SDA, from the Muslim side, were being abused at HVO checkpoints, on one occasion one had been killed, and a particularly important one had been imprisoned. If there couldn't be a presentation of these representatives at the table, then any -- any thought of discussions around a table would have been quite impossible. We had to resolve the blocking points before we could make a mechanism work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Beese, you mentioned propaganda. Can you tell the Trial Chamber which party or parties engaged in what might be termed propaganda?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a degree of propaganda on both sides, I should say at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. By "both sides," which sides are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat and Muslim elements both used propaganda to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how do you define propaganda? What do you mean by that term?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Propaganda is passing a message, spreading dogma in order to encourage others to support your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe some examples of propaganda that you became aware of while serving as an ECMM monitor in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Propaganda took many forms. I believe it was essential for the HVO to ensure that their people and supporters had a consistent message. Verbally to us their constant reference to Muslim aggression was propaganda aimed at determining our opinion as to who is right, if you like, or who is wrong, or who is responsible for violence. There was also propaganda spread to the peoples of Herzegovina through media, whether that is press or television. There is the raising of flags. There is the presentation of -- of values. I can't say whether they were official or not, but the display of pictures of Ante Pavlovic and symbols of Ustasha not only publicly displayed but in the offices of HV officials was designed to produce a message. There were messages given. On occasion at meetings I had with HVO officials, on occasion Mr. Tadic -- I arrived at a meeting to find a television crew was there. The crew filmed our discussion, filmed him leading me from office to office. The -- our conversation and discussions were not recorded and therefore the images, I believe, were used to give an impression that we were supporting and supportive of Mr. Tadic's policies. The wording applied to the transmission would have been at the television's choice rather than what we actually said. The same was the case at a meeting I had with Mr. Maric in Grude, where Mr. Maric was addressing a meeting of relatives of people who had been held captive by the Serb forces in -- predominantly in the Banja Luka area where the meeting was televised. I believe that it was designed to show that we supported Mr. Maric's call for humanitarian effort in releasing these prisoners to support the HVO position that they were an aggrieved party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, you mentioned, or testified as reflected on lines 21 and 22 of page 54, that propaganda was spread to the peoples of Herzegovina. Were you aware of any propaganda in other areas covered by regional centre Zenica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Propaganda takes many forms. Propaganda can be used, for instance, by the use of specific words. The word "Mujahedin" itself can be used as propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: By both parties. One party can suggest, for instance, if you -- if you announce to a Croat village that the Mujahedin were about to come over the hill, you could reasonably expect the villagers to take flight. They had no reason to wait for the Mujahedin to turn up, with all that the word "Mujahedin" meant, to see what their intentions were. But likewise, in the southern area, if you said that Tuta was coming, that was bad news. You weren't going to get the sort of hearing you might get from an organised unit of the HVO. You were going to be subject to the determination of Tuta. That was bad news. So the use of these words, whether to encourage people to fly or to condemn another party by referring to Mujahedin, for instance, is in itself a form of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And these two examples that you've given, Mr. Beese, of propaganda relating to the Mujahedin and propaganda relating to Tuta, which party or parties were employing these two specific lines of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO referred to Mujahedin in meetings that I had with them, specifically a meeting with Mr. Prlic. Other more junior HVO officials referred to Muslim extremists and Mujahedin. I raised the matter with Valentin Coric who had complained about extreme Muslim elements, the Mujahedin in Central Bosnia. I asked him how they came to be in Central Bosnia, as almost any movement into and out of Central Bosnia was governed by HVO and their checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, based on your work as an ECMM monitor, did you see any effects of this propaganda?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two effects. The first to convince the people of Herzegovina that the Muslims were indeed extreme. It would have been very difficult, given my understanding of the bond within families in Herzegovina, those that I met, they were not keen to send their sons to war unless there was just cause for this war. Muslim aggression justified defence, and therefore by broadcasting details of Muslim aggression by any means would encourage families to release their -- their sons, husbands, fathers for the fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You indicated two effects. That was the first. Do you recall a second effect?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second effect was the just cause of territorial claim. The use of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, for instance, to demonstrate Croat ownership of provinces, and to some extent to convince people of success. Whilst engaged in the Gornji Vakuf cease-fire and withdrawal talks, I returned to Siroki Brijeg one night to find that whilst we had or were discussing active cease-fire and withdrawal it was pointed out to me by two people that on television in our base, that the mayor of Siroki Brijeg was pictured urging his troops on, that is those that were -- had come from Siroki Brijeg to Gornji Vakuf, in -- in the fight. And to see them urging on at a time when we were actively discussing cease-fire was extraordinary, and I can only believe that the -- the importance of that was to demonstrate that the HVO or the Croats had not been beaten and were still doing a good job at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, did you notice, as an ECMM monitor, were there any noticeable effects of propaganda by the HVO in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO in Central Bosnia would use flags to show that territory was theirs. The routine use of flags was extremely provocative. They would raise a flag wherever they had a post, whether that post was manned by a thousand men or simply two. And the continued raising of flags of one particular party in a federation, particularly on the interface between the two peoples, which Central Bosnia might seem to have been, was inflammatory. The raising of the HVO flags in Travnik during Mr. Boban's visit had specifically sparked protests and violence. So the raising of flags raised tension but demonstrated to people that there was a Croatian presence and some success.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your recollection, Mr. Beese, were -- was the subject of propaganda covered in ECMM reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The raising of flags was. The -- some of the incidents that I've referred to with television coverage were also recorded, but I can't refer to specific reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown P 02692.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see that document on the screen before you, Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a message from the Danish delegation of the ECMM in Zagreb to a gentleman whose name is unfamiliar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we please turn to page 7 of this document. Can you, please, Mr. Beese -- actually, we want page 7. Sorry, if you could go forward two more pages. The cover page -- I'm looking for the page with the number 7 at the bottom. Can you tell me, Mr. Beese -- I would like you to look at the section headed 8.6, "RC Zenica reports." And particularly the first two paragraphs of that part. If you could take a look at that, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this special report -- or what this report is referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerns the conflict in Travnik and the withdrawal of Croatian people from Travnik and from some surrounding villages into stronger pockets, in particular Busovaca and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the second paragraph under that section?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerns the allegations of atrocity in some of the Croat villages that people had fled from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd now ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P 02849.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see that document, Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Capsat report from the head of regional centre Zenica, Ambassador Thebault, to the headquarters of ECMM in Zagreb, particularly to the Head of Mission, to the Deputy Head of Mission, chief operating officer and humanitarian cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you know what this document concerns?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the situation it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it refers to, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports that we received from our teams in Travnik were to the effect that the Croats in Travnik had withdrawn their civilian population prior to a military assault. The military assault failed. The HVO announced that the Muslim element had driven their people out of Travnik. We believe this was not correct and that therefore this was propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we please go to the top of page 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The print's a little small for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could get that enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention, sir, to the first -- approximately the first ten lines or so under paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, can you elaborate on anything that's written in this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have access to HVO policy directly. I've not been briefed by the HVO, but it did appear to us that they had a desire to withdraw their people from areas that might later be considered pockets and to move their people to areas in which they were stronger. There were two reasons to do this: First of all, they could better make use of people in stronger communities that they could defend. Secondly, it would change the voting pattern in that area in Croat favour. The use of propaganda, the claims that the Mujahedin were coming, was one way of encouraging Croats to leave their homes. The second is a direct order to move out of their homes. There were occasions known to me when Croats wished to move to a different centre. On one occasion we were aware that Croat civilians wished to move from the Vitez-Busovaca area up into Zenica where they may have felt safer and better looked after than in the pockets. We understood from witnesses that they were prevented from doing this by the Vojna Policija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, a few moments ago you mentioned reports concerning Travnik. Do you recall whether there were any ECMM reports that were specifically produced concerning events in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had based a team, a competent and experienced team in Travnik at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who were -- who were the members of this competent and experienced team that was in Travnik at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Torbjorn Junhof was the head of the coordination centre there, a Swedish officer, supported by Philip Watkins, a British officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, what type of information they were reporting from the Travnik area? Well, first of all, let me ask you the time period. Let me ask you to focus on the time period in June, 1993. Do you recall any of the events that they were reporting in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They witnessed the onset of open conflict in Travnik from which they were withdrawn by UNPROFOR. They then patrolled the villages around the area of Travnik to ascertain what was actually happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was done with the information that Mr. Watkins and Mr. Junhof reported to the regional centre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hate to interrupt but I think we'll lose quite a lot of time if we deal with Travnik. Travnik is not in the indictment, as far as I know. I think that that part of the story is a little irrelevant, or are we opening up the question again of what is and what is not in the indictment, but Travnik is definitely not in the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes. Mr. Mundis, what is your objective in pursuing the subject of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Travnik, as you -- as you are all too familiar, is in Central Bosnia and of course the regional centre Zenica was reporting on events in Travnik, but I will move on. I would ask that the witness be shown a document which is marked P 02168.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And while that's coming up on the screen, let me ask you this,

utterances.speaker: MR. BEESE
utterances.text: What type of political reporting, if any, was ECMM doing during the time period you were Deputy Head of Mission?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were required to report on political matters of the moment, in particular in June, July on Vance-Owen Peace Plan and the -- the municipal structures in place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you now see, sir, the document that's before you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Capsat report from Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault to the headquarters of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what is the subject of this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political and military situation in middle -- Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before, Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What would have been the basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm referring to relevance once again. I agree the ECMM office in Zenica was active in that area, and geographically it's all referred to as Central Bosnia. However, in the indictment only Gornji Vakuf and Prozor are mentioned in Central Bosnia. Now we're going to be talking about Zenica, Travnik, perhaps Vitez and Busovaca again, and so on and so forth. I think that if we are dealing with these documents, we should focus on the parts dealing with the towns mentioned in the indictment. Geographically, they are part of Central Bosnia, but this is another part of Central Bosnia, and it's not in our indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then go on to ask your question about towns that are in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. President. It's a bit unclear to me whether I should proceed or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, proceed, but focus on what is contained in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just briefly respond that of course the Prosecution's allegations do concern the policies of the HVO and that those policies, as this witness has testified about over the course of the past two days, included certain elements within Central Bosnia. There have been issues discussed concerning Central Bosnia. So we're simply showing this witness some document or a document concerning the political and military situation in an area that we believe is part of this case in terms of HVO policies has been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So again, Mr. Beese, can you tell us what would have been the basis for this report, P 02168, that was prepared by the head of the regional centre Zenica, Ambassador Thebault?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see, please, a little more of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would you like to see the following page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, before we answer the question, if I may. I'm just a little troubled by Mr. Mundis's previous answer. I hesitate to react today because I felt that yesterday perhaps I reacted more than the Bench wanted me to, but in this instance it would appear now that matters are being discussed and evidence is being brought in that is not necessarily in the indictment. However, it's going to be used somehow to either enlarge the indictment at the end of the trial. I really have a very difficult time understanding what is the purpose of talking about a policy that is outside this indictment. You know, is this for context purposes? Maybe it's because of my Anglo-Saxon background, training, that I don't understand this form of drafting indictments, but it seems like everything, including the kitchen sink now, is being thrown at us, and I need to know with specificity what it is that I am -- that I need to respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But let's hear the question first, because you're anticipating something that we don't know yet what we're going to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Judges have just remarked that in the indictment there's the general thesis of the joint criminal enterprise with all its different aspects and facets, and one should focus on that issue as well, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I might take the opportunity, since the joint criminal enterprise was brought up, that is -- that is even more the reason, that is even more the reason - I underscore that - when it comes to cross-examination the Trial Chamber must be very mindful to allow the Defence every opportunity to explore all of these issues as opposed to limiting us as it has been, albeit sometimes we call it crime base, but I think this underscores the complexities that Defence is facing with respect to putting limitations on cross-examination. And I want to thank Judge Trechsel for pointing out the fact that this goes to the general concept of -- of what I would call the beast of joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may add two words. [Interpretation] Even if we use the facts concerning the region of Central Bosnia within the context of this indictment, as we know from judgements in other cases, the circumstances and the events are not the same as those mentioned in our indictment. All of Central Bosnia was surrounded by the BH army -- excuse me. Not all, but a large part, the northern part; Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca. They were totally encircled. So the context must be different, and this has been established in other cases. So it is not possible for the context to be the same. Therefore we cannot mention this in the same context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Continue, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Beese, was actually upon what basis did Ambassador Thebault draft this report that you see before you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Thebault produced the report from evidence produced to him from his teams on the ground. It endeavoured to show the situation in Central Bosnia. And whilst one talks of Central Bosnia, I mean particularly the Lasva Valley. We believed that the chain of HVO-controlled municipalities along the Lasva Valley had a relevance not only to the Lasva Valley but to provinces 8 and 10. They were not separate from, they were a part of that. Indeed, they formed the northern flank, if you wish to call it that, and boundaries of provinces 8 and 10. Therefore, what happened in the Lasva Valley was directly relevant to what happened south of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I would like to ask you now, again, based upon your observations, if you were able to reach some conclusions or ideas about what the HVO goals were. Again, based on your observations.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With particular relevance to this region, the Lasva Valley, there was a need for three things: The first was to withdraw Croat civilians forcibly or voluntarily behind, that is south of the -- of the line into provinces 8 and 10. By causing a degree of confusion by attacks, by propaganda, it both encouraged Croats to leave their areas and return south. It also supported the view that there was Muslim aggression. Ultimately, it seemed to us the purpose of the Croatian communities along that line - Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez - were, if you like, the border, the front line. These people were responsible for drawing the attention of -- and preventing incursion by 3rd Corps of the armija south to support units around Jablanica. They were, if you like, a screen to prevent reinforcement of the relief of Jablanica and the Konjic area by 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, in the wider area of Herzegovina, based on your observations, what did it appear to you to be the goals of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goals appear to be the establishment of a mini-state and that Herceg-Bosna would not simply be a concept but would be a mini-state, and would be a mini-state that had all the necessary instruments of government, of an operating economy, jobs for people, and a specific way of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you personally, Mr. Beese, observe any steps being taken in this direction?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the issues of culture, the raising of flags, the matters of education, passports, number plates, demonstrated that a desired way of life was to be implemented. The concentration of votes and therefore political control through the movement of Croat civilians would support the state definition of borders of that through control of all territory south of the Lasva Valley, the attempt to secure all parts of the power producing mechanism from the source of water in Lake Ramsko, the hydroelectric facility towards Jablanica and south on the Neretva and control of the factories below would produce an economy which would pay people's wages and earn currency from export of power and products to other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I'd now like to turn your attention to an entirely different subject. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you were here in The Hague last week or not.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for how long -- when did you arrive and when did you depart?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent two days in The Hague last week; Wednesday and Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, during that time period you met with my colleague Mr. Bos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And among other things, you were asked to review a large number of documents.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately how many documents you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed something in the region of five lever-arch files.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you have an idea, approximately how many documents were contained in these five lever-arch files?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not by number of documents. A significant number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how long, Mr. Beese, did you review these documents provided by Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to show that the documents were, to the best of my knowledge, the product or through-put of the ECMM. I was not required to read them word-for-word, simply to support the view that they were ECMM source documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to go through these binders?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many of the documents in the binders did you actually look at?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at every single page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the five binders that you reviewed contained what type of documents?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Principally ECMM reports of the type we've seen on the screen today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what -- can you be more specific when you say "ECMM reports of the type we've seen on the screen today"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority were Capsat reports from RC Zenica and its supporting teams to Zagreb, and a number from Zagreb on beyond to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if you remember, sir, the reports that you reviewed, what were their frequency?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- there were daily reports, there were weekly summaries, and there were special reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the ECMM reports, whether daily, weekly, or summary, special reports, what other types of documents, if any, were contained in the five binders?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of documents which were not ECMM documents or products but which had been passed by ECMM from the theatre to other destinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of a type of document that was not an ECMM document but which had been passed by ECMM from the field?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Copies of letters sent to the ECMM or relevant to the ECMM by the parties, either from Mr. Arif Pasalic, for instance, in Mostar, or from Mr. Boban or Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the time period of the documents in the five binders that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were approximately from the time of my arrival to some months after I departed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the geographic scope of the reports contained in the five binders that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina as controlled by the forces of the BiH or HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which -- if you recall, sir, which regional centres were covered by the documents -- regional centre or centres, that were covered by the documents in the five binders?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those relating to RC Zenica, whether it was based in Split or Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you reviewed the documents, Mr. Beese, did you direct Mr. Bos to remove any of the documents?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of documents, not very many, but some which I could not substantiate or indicate were part of the ECMM reporting process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those documents?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bos removed them from the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based upon your review of these documents, Mr. Beese, the documents provided by Mr. Bos, what conclusions did you reach about the material contained in the five binders?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Mr. Bos had assembled a number of critical documents. They were a selection, they were by no means, of course, all the reports issued at the time, but they covered many of the matters pertinent to affairs in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know that they covered many of the matters pertinent to affairs in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was party to those affairs myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And with respect to those affairs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I may just add a question. Would you say, sir, that this also applies to reports filed at the time when you had already left the area? Would you still consider that you were a party to the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, I was not party. I simply confirmed to Mr. Bos that I was aware of the personalities and could confirm their presence in theatre at that time and that the content of the messages was consistent with my understanding of affairs, which did not change greatly in the months after I left, and that the tone of the -- or the -- the way the reports had been written was consistent with the styles applied by the various monitors who compiled the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will need to touch upon this at some point after Mr. Mundis finishes. I take it he's laying a foundation, but I do want to touch back on this because I believe the gentleman has speculated about reports that were generated after he left, and I would like to know on what basis - because he wasn't in the field - other than pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I believe there's a mistake in line 17 in part of your answer. I believe that what you said was the way the reports had been written was consistent with the styles applied by the various monitors.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What's the basis for that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many monitors, of course, came from countries other than those that speak English as their first language, therefore their particular use of English phrases is particular. It doesn't mean to say it's wrong or inaccurate, but they have a particular style and choice of words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beese.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take it, if I may, based on this presentation from -- from -- the last serious of questions by Mr. Mundis, which perhaps in my opinion should have been done at the beginning of the direct examination, but far from me -- far be it from me to give advice to the Prosecution, this was a basis for laying the foundation for which all these other documents will be coming in. If I may, just on this very, very narrow issue, unless the Trial Chamber wishes to do so, I would like to conduct what we could call a voir dire, a questioning on a limited basis, because at some point we may be asked whether we're going to have any objections as to the documents coming in. And so I would ask, or I would ask the Trial Chamber to ask, for instance, whether he can vouch to any degree of certainty - of course under oath - that these documents are authentic, number one; and number two, are reliable. In other words, they haven't been altered in any fashion. And especially as to documents that may have been generated after he left the field. I know that he's talking about reading through the tea leaves, that, yes, this is the same phraseology that folks that come from various countries might use, but that doesn't necessarily mean that the document itself has -- is authentic or reliable. So I would like that to be asked, and also perhaps some questions as to the chain of custody: Where were these documents kept? Who were the custodians? Where are these archives? And so on and so forth. I think those are critical issues, and perhaps also, since we have the gentleman here, whether Mr. Bos also has other documents that it might be relevant to the entire case, not just for the Prosecution, or that might go to his mindset as to what the events were and who was responsible for certain incidents in Central Bosnia or other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the critical period of the indictment. So I would be more than happy to conduct this mini-voir dire, as it were, or perhaps the Trial Chamber might wish to ask these questions. I'm merely making the suggestion and request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Karnavas, you're going to begin with your cross-examination, and within the cross-examination you can, of course, ask the witness document by document, the ones admitted or your documents, you can ask him about the authenticity of the documents, but that comes at the cross-examination stage. During the Prosecutor's stage with the documents and the authenticity of the document, if you feel that the document is a false one, and then you can take that matter up, and if you doubt the authenticity of the document, then you'll be able to ask the witness about it. Otherwise, the documents that were presented to the witness, you were all able to note that they had the ECMM stamp on the documents, and all the documents also have the time, the hour, minutes, second when they were sent out to Zagreb or elsewhere. So there are a number of elements on the basis of which we are able to conclude that those documents come from the authority mentioned on the document itself. Except if you think that certain passages have been falsified, and then it's up to you to prove it. Otherwise, all the characteristics of the document point to the fact that they were ECMM and that they were officially sent to the Prosecutor through official channels from the ECMM to the Prosecution. So there's an international authority transmitting the documents to the Prosecution. And it might seem -- it would seem unbelievable that this authority would falsify documents, but perhaps you have reason to believe this to be true. If so, it's up to you to prove it and not to throw out these statements without proving them, make the allegations without proving them. So you haven't got the originals. Most of the time they are copies, of course. They are faxes as well, or documents sent out through electronic communication. So they are in a copy form. They are not the originals as such. Counsel Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First and foremost, I want to make sure that the record is very clear that no allegations have been made. Secondly, I do have experience with this particular organisation in being rather uncooperative in my experience in providing access to its archives. We don't have access to everything. And I don't have access to all the originals. Be that as it may, it has been the practice in other Trial Chambers not to admit any documents until after the cross-examination, thereby allowing both parties to present their positions. In other words, the Prosecution would ask the Court which documents -- or the Court would ask the Prosecution which documents it wishes to tender, it would then turn to the Defence to see whether there would be any objections. The objections might be noted for the record for appeal purposes, even under this particular system, and then the Trial Chamber would make a decision whether a document would come in or not, and of course if the Defence would be objecting to a particular document on authenticity, it would be up to the Defence or to the party who is objecting to demonstrate as to why that document would not come in. So there are no accusations being made. On the other hand, I'm a Defence lawyer, and I take nothing and no one at their word. I'm entitled to challenge. At this point in time the gentleman wishes to bring in -- or the Prosecution is going to bring in documents which were generated after the gentleman was with this particular organisation. I merely wish to have one particular question posed to this witness, whether, based on observing these documents, can he with any degree of certainty tell us whether these documents are indeed authentic, and are they reliable? Those are two very -- questions. I think it's not unreasonable and nothing should be read into those. So I'm not suggesting that this organisation or any other organisation is trying to do anything in particular, and if I conveyed that, I apologise to the gentleman and to the organisation, although it has been uncooperative with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The questions that have just been raised can be raised before the start of the cross-examination. It is obvious that you're going to be allowed to ask questions of that nature, but you should go ahead and ask them at the start of the cross-examination. We're not going to raise them now and then wait two months before continuing. So keep your ammunition for the beginning of the cross-examination. Now, I'm looking at Mr. Mundis. What are the exhibits that you're going to ask to be tendered into evidence, admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: All of these documents, Mr. President. We're asking that all of these, these five finders, the approximately 40 documents that were shown to the witness, the witness's account, we're asking -- we will be tendering all of these documents. It might be easier for us to produce a spreadsheet with the information. I don't believe it's a particularly useful exercise for me to read into the record several hundred numbers of documents we propose to tender into evidence, but it is our intention, through this witness and his testimony over the past two days, that all of these documents are relevant, reliable, have probative value, and should be admitted into evidence. And I'm fully aware that the Defence are going to respond to the written document we filed today but it's certainly our position, Mr. President and Your Honours, that all these documents be admitted into evidence based on this witness's testimony. I want to make that absolutely clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Karnavas, before I give you the floor. To summarise, you presented a first set of documents beginning with 1.215, and it goes on to 9.607, and those exhibits were presented to the witness who commented on them on the basis of your questions and in response to your questions. So this is recapitulation. Then you also presented a document which was not in this set here, in this binder, but was in the other pile that I have to my left, and this morning you questioned the witness about some of them. You're now saying, officially, that you're going to ask that all the documents be tendered into evidence, that is to say those on the list plus the others, not all of which were presented to the witness. Those not presented to the witness, with the exception of one such document, will be the subject of a written submission from you, and the Defence will be responding to the procedure of admission without having the documents presented, and then also with respect to the relevance and ultimately the probative value and weight of those documents. So I have just summarised the situation at ten minutes past twelve. Mr. Mundis, could you tell me if I have got the situation right and summarised it properly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps it's an interpretation problem. Our position, Mr. President, is that these documents, the materials in the five binders, were presented to the witness but were not done in court. That is, the witness sat down, as he testified about, and reviewed them. So we would -- we would ask that it be reflected in the record that our position is they were presented to the witness but not in court, and he described -- he testified about the procedure that was taken out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. Yes. I'm going to give the floor to Counsel Karnavas, but when I personally looked at this yesterday, and I think my colleagues will agree, in my mind when I discussed this, the documents between Mr. Bos and the witness, and you told us how he went through them with Mr. Bos, because we still have some time left, you could present them very quickly to the witness in the presence of the Defence counsel before this Trial Chamber. We could take binder number 1, and you could say we have Exhibit 626, ECMM. Yes, I recognise it. Then go on: 954, ECMM document; yes, I confirm that. And then you could go through these documents in front of everyone, and that's what I suggested you do yesterday. You preferred to follow a different line. Counsel Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I feel like we're on the same wavelength right now, because I was just going to say why can't they just do it on the record? I take them at their word that they went through the documents with the gentleman, but we need to make a record, and albeit we had some questions being asked for foundational purposes, I think it's much better to have the witness go through the binders. We can go through -- we do have some time because we're scheduled to be here until 1.45. Go through them. And of course I would then ask at the conclusion of all of this, I would still ask that though they are tendered they not be admitted into evidence until after the conclusion of the cross-examination. That's all I'm asking. But I do think that it would be clearer and nicer, since we have the witness here, to just go through the -- through the -- we can take a little break. I understand Mr. Mundis is up on his feet but perhaps is a little tired also from having to prepare for this witness, but after the break I'm sure he can rejuvenate himself so we can go through these documents, make our record, and then it's the way you proposed it, Mr. President. I think that's a good process for the rest of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I will give you the floor, but Counsel Karnavas has just put forward a suggestion which agrees with the one I made yesterday, coincides with that, and that is that -- yes, we're going to take a break now, but when we reconvene, we put your binder to the witness so that he can see it and then he can say 626, yes, 500 et cetera, yes, I have seen the document, I confirm it, and so on and so forth. When we get through them all, the Chamber, as also suggested by the Defence, will see. After the cross-examination, the Chamber will give a definitive ruling and then there will be no problem. [In English] What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if it takes us one minute per document, it will take about six and a half hours to do that. If it takes 30 seconds, it will take us about four more hours. I'm happy to do that, but really, Mr. President, with all due respect, I'm not sure it's the best use of the Trial Chamber's time. Again, the witness has testified about what he did. There is a record of what he has done with respect to these documents. However, perhaps during the recess I can consult with my colleagues and we can see what we can do about using the remaining time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In actual fact, if we need the e-court system, it will take a long time, but if you take the binder physically and place it before the witness's eyes, then we'll be able to follow it all, 626, and all the other numbers. It will just take a second. So my solution would be to place the hard copy in front of the witness and then you can say 626, okay; 954, okay; et cetera, onwards, and we could get through it very quickly. We won't need six hours. Mr. Scott, I said that you sent in a written submission. It can, of course, be orally modified to suit the development of events, and the Prosecution always has to adapt itself to be adapted to the latest developments. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Apology to my colleague Mr. Mundis. I intervene because this is an issue that doesn't relate only to Mr. Beese but will relate to a number witnesses in the future, and indeed there will be a witness coming next week from another organisation which we will propose and handle exactly same way that we have done with this witness unless and until the Trial Chamber gives us very clear instructions to the contrary. Your Honour, with all respect, this would be an incredible waste of time. The witness has testified under oath, under oath - and there is no reason to say he's lying - that he did this. He said he looked at every document, and he confirmed that they were ECMM documents. He went through every one. He said he went through every single one. Now, if Mr. Karnavas has some reason to think that Mr. Beese is lying, put the question, put the basis to the witness and ask him. Why should we spend -- you have limited the Prosecution to 400 hours to present our case. Now, why should we spend any part of our 400 hours going through one document at a time, 350; is that correct; is that correct; is that correct? The witness has done it. He testified to it under oath, and unless Mr. Karnavas or some other Defence counsel has a reason to say this man is lying and he didn't do that, then the record has been made. There is a record in the case that this has been done. He's identified it, he's so testified. We can ask him again if he did it and we can say what we already did, and he can say it again: I reviewed every document with Mr. Bos last week and I confirmed that all the ones except for the ones that were removed were ECMM documents. He's already testified to that. There is no reason to believe that that is false.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may just propose a solution -- a solution. And first of all, I think Mr. Scott ought to keep his powder dry. Nobody is accusing anybody of lying, and I take offence to that. I take offence to that. It is highly unprofessional. Another solution would be, since they're in binders, for the gentleman, over the break, to look at them and then Mr. Mundis can say, In binder number 1, going from this number to that number, did you review them? Yes, and so on and so forth. That's -- that's another solution. It's not document by document, but where I come from you go through every document every single time, and perhaps the Prosecution should not have as many documents. That's not my fault. They chose this approach, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where Mr. Karnavas practised law but that's what we do where I come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. The practical solution would be to take a break now. We could have a half-hour break, slightly longer, and then the witness can go through the binder again and I myself will be asking him when we reconvene, asking him whether the documents he saw in the binder correspond to what he told Mr. Bos, to know that they are ECMM documents, that some of them he knew while he was on duty in the field, others that he didn't know of but that he did know that they were official documents, and so on. So perhaps we could settle that question that way. Yes, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I'd just like to mention that the Defence does not have the files, the binders. So once again, if we apply this method, the method that you yourself as the learned Judge have proposed, we won't be able to control the proceedings because we don't have the binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you don't have the binders, I can give you my own. That way you'll have the documents and you'll have half an hour to go through the documents. Mr. Mundis, the Defence -- well, yes. They have the numbers but they don't have them in front of their eyes. So if you have an extra binder, provide me with one. I'll give them the Chamber's binder so that they have a chance to go through it. I won't need half an hour to go through all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have one set of the materials here, which I need to give to the witness, or if the witness is going to be asked to review them over the break, then he needs a set. Mr. Bos apparently has another set in his office we can provide, I guess, to the Defence at the break. Of course, they're all in e-court and they can print them all out, but we'll provide a copy to the Defence, and I would ask that the usher then provide Mr. Beese with a set of all five binders of the documents during the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have two sets of documents, one set that can be given to the witness and another set that can be given to the Defence. If you don't have sufficient copies, I'm happy to place my documents at the disposal of the Defence counsels. So we all have half an hour to go through them. It is now 20 minutes past twelve. We reconvene in half an hour's time, that is to say approximately ten to one, and I hope you have a good half-hour reading time. Yes, Witness. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, so we can establish the basis upon which I pass these documents, I pass these documents on the basis that I understood the subject matter, I understood the markings such as destinations and transmission, and I had no reason to believe these were anything other than legitimate ECMM communication. I could not, of course, validate that they were the transmission of the time as I was not in theatre through the entire period. Is that sufficient for your needs, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Obviously we understood that you weren't in theatre during some of these documents, when some of these documents were compiled. That's what I said yesterday. But you can look through the documents now and say, yes, this is an ECMM document, and everybody will know and understand that you weren't actually there. So you can do no more than that. So it's 12.20. We reconvene at ten minutes to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us resume the hearing. I take note of the fact that the witness was able to go through the binders in the almost 40 minutes that we had of a break, and I should like to take note that the Defence also had a chance to look through those documents, albeit quickly. Mr. Beese, can you confirm that during those 40 minutes you were able to consult the five binders that you were provided with by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can you confirm for the record that those binders contain documents which are numbered, they have reference numbers, and you were able to go through those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was able to go through them, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Among the documents that you went through, were there documents relating to the time period that you were on duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and were there also documents which were drafted after your departure from Bosnia-Herzegovina? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the record once again, could you tell me when you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina and when you left Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 8th or 9th of January, 2000 -- 1993, and I departed on the 21st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you arrived on the 8th of January, 1993, and you departed on the 21st of July, 1993. Now, among the documents that you looked through, were there documents which were drafted before you arrived in January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there documents that were drafted after your departure on the 21st of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the documents drafted after your departure, were there documents that emanated from the European Mission that originated from the ECMM, and were there other documents as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there were, to both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents drafted after your departure, did they relate to events which you yourself had knowledge of ex officio, or did they refer to individuals whom you might have met at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They related to events that I was familiar with, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having examined all the binders, as far as you're concerned are there any documents which to your mind have nothing to do with the events that you were familiar with, or are you telling us that all the documents that were presented by Mr. Bos to you and which you were able to go through relate to the period that you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, on examination, there are four documents within these files for which I cannot show there is any connection with the ECMM. It does not mean to say that they are not relevant material, but I cannot demonstrate that they are part of the ECMM means of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And those four documents, can you give me the references, the reference numbers, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Document 09044. Also document 02935. Also document 03346. And finally, document 03539.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the document 9044, 2935, 3346, and 3539, in your opinion have nothing to do with the ECMM, but you do not exclude the possibility of them being pertinent and relevant; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now to make up for lost time, but my colleague has a question before we do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you say anything about the authenticity of these four documents? Whether they are authentic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So on the basis of what has been stated -- Mr. Mundis, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. President. Although these four numbered documents were clearly in the binders that Mr. Beese had, I just note at this point in time they are not on the list and they are not among the materials that were provided to the Trial Chamber. So I believe that the copy that Mr. Beese had inadvertently had some documents which apparently Mr. Bos did not remove from the set that the witness reviewed. But just to be clear for the record, the four numbers he read out are not among the documents that are included on the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So that was a mistake. They were documents that normally would not have been presented. So you're saying that those four documents are not on the list that you would like to have tendered into evidence. I'm now looking at the Defence. Are there any observations that anybody would like to make? Counsel Ibrisimovic, quickly, please

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. On the list of documents that the Defence was provided on the 13th of June, there are four documents which were drafted before the witness arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They date back to the beginning of 1992 and 1993 when the witness was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know whether the witness has seen those documents, but I have them on the list. They are the first four documents on our spreadsheet, or list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if I ask the question it is because I noticed that myself. Mr. Beese, the Defence has just noted that there are four documents which were drafted before your arrival. Perhaps you had knowledge of those documents once you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could you refer to those four documents for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Counsel Ibrisimovic, could you give us the reference numbers of those documents, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 626 is the 24th of October, 1992, ECMM, relating to the activities of the 23rd of October, 1992. The next document, 954, is a document that was drafted at 18.18, addressed to Zenica, and is a report which concerns Christmas Day, 1992. Document 1045 is a message for the Danish delegation to Zagreb. The date is the 2nd of January, 1993. It says "priority." And the fourth document, 1050, is a document which begins at the 4th -- on the 4th of January at 18.15 hours and goes up to the 31st of August -- well, actually there are a number of entries. Mr. Beese, those documents, what about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, taking 1050 first, that is, I believe, a diary written by an ECMM monitor, covering the period that I was in the region. Although it is first dated the 4th of January, I did arrive on the 2nd of January in theatre. So it does cover the same period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They do refer to events before my arrival. They are matters that I was generally aware of, but I agree, I apologise, they were prepared and transmitted before my arrival, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for those precisions. The rest of the Defence team. No observations from the Defence? Then the Chamber, which deliberated, considers that on the one hand there were documents that are being tendered, documents presented by the Prosecution which begin with 1215, and that is this binder here with the table, so these are documents that have been recognised, and they are admitted. All the other documents in the other files and binders, those documents will have an identification number, marked for identification, and the Chamber will only give a ruling on the documents at the end of the cross-examination. But it would like to suggest to the Prosecution that they indicate, when the time comes, which documents they would like to present to other witnesses or introduce through other witnesses, particularly those that were drafted after the witness's departure in 1993. So we're going to have the cross-examination, after which we will decide and give a ruling, and it is up to the Prosecution to tell us whether among the list of documents there are those that might be introduced through another witness or other witnesses. We will also make a ruling on the written submissions that have been filed, and we of course invite the Defence to submit their written submissions, collectively, perhaps, within a 10-day deadline, shall we say? Try and send them in as soon as possible so we can deliberate and on that basis make a ruling in the matter, because the question might arise and will probably arise another time. Mr. Beese, that completes your examination-in-chief. You will be recalled to the Tribunal at a date to be made known to you by the Registrar for the cross-examination stage, and then you will be, of course, answering questions put to you by the Defence counsel and any of the accused who wish to ask you any questions. It will be in a few weeks' time, so the Defence and the accused will have a chance to prepare themselves for the cross-examination. Between now and then, you are to have no contact with the Prosecution or members of the Defence teams, because having made the solemn declaration, you are now a witness of the justice system. So you're in a rather specific situation. So please don't make contact and have contacts either with the Prosecution, which has completed its examination-in-chief. That's how we stand now. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I probably should have jumped up a minute or two earlier. I did explain to Mr. Beese that he would have to come back, and actually in order to check some available dates with Mr. Beese, we are proposing that Mr. Beese return for cross-examination commencing on Monday, the 14th of August, 2006. That would be immediately upon the return from the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the date might be an excellent date indeed, however, I understood it -- as I understood it, the Defence, with respect to the 15th of August, would prefer it if we were to take up our proceedings again on the 16th of August. And I see Mr. Karnavas would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Actually, if we could have it, like, on the 17th, because for those of us who are practising our religion, the 15th of August, both in the Greek Orthodox and the Roman Catholic religions, that's a very large holiday. It's usually the third largest holiday after Christmas and Easter, being Madonna Day. That's the one reason. Hopefully by that point in time we will have the translations. I particularly don't like to have Mr. Beese come right then. I would prefer him coming later only because, obviously while the Prosecution will be basking in the sun and relaxing, we're going to be busy having to prepare for Mr. Beese. I spoke with some of my colleagues, and it would appear that the cross-examination is going to take an extensive period of time. I think, by my estimation, I alone will need four to five days with Mr. Beese. I think some of the others may wish to have a day or two, but I think in total it's nearly ten days that we're going to be asking Mr. Beese to be cross-examined in light of the length and the breadth of his direct examination. He went into all sorts of areas; military, political, economic, and so on and so forth. So anyway, I just bring that out. And again, at this time I would want to make this oral application that we start perhaps on the 17th so that those of us who might be in another country for this particular holiday would have a chance to get back, you know, and I certainly would appreciate that because of my elderly relatives, and this is one of the days that I usually visit every year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an oral submission, first of all the matter of the 15th, and you would like to see us begin on the 17th of August. That's the first possibility. But there's a second possibility which was raised, and that is that you would prepare to start on the 17th of August but not straight away with this witness because you have all the intellectual preparations that go with the cross-examination, and you have the right, just like anybody else does, a few days of rest. So you feel that it would be better if the cross-examination of this witness should not start on the 17th of August but perhaps we could have another witness on the 17th of August, which would allow you to go ahead a few days later. Mr. Mundis, that was the gist of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Certainly the scheduling matters are entirely a matter for the Trial Chamber. We would certainly, given the fact that we spent barely more than five and a half hours, we would certainly, for the record, oppose any cross-examination that will last five or seven or 10 days with respect to Mr. Beese, and I want that made very clear on the record at this point in time. We can certainly endeavour to bring another witness in on the 17th. I'm not sure if we would be sitting on Friday the 18th of that week. If not, then I will endeavour to bring in a very short crime base witness and that would be the only witness we would have that week. Again, if Mr. Beese is available the following week, we would bring him at that point in time. I also note that we are a two months away from this proposed cross-examination and there is adequate time, in our respectful views, for the Defence to both have a few days' rest and to prepare for the cross-examination of this witness. So, again, we would oppose, for the record right now, any cross-examination lasting the amount of time Mr. Karnavas has suggested. I'm at the Trial Chamber's liberty. I would appreciate hearing from whether we're sitting only the 17th during that week and I will endeavour to bring in a short crime base witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, as to the duration of the cross-examination, as you know the Appeals Chamber will be making a ruling on that score, so let's wait to hear what the Appeals Chamber has to say, and after that we will determine the time that will be allocated to all the teams for the cross-examination. So that remains to be seen. The Chamber does not want to rule on that today because we shall wait to hear the ruling by the Appeals Chamber. Once we have heard it, we will be able to tell you how long the cross-examination will last. I think that we all understand that now. Mr. Mundis has just told us that to all intents and purposes he could get a crime base witness for the 17th. So what about the following week, the week after that? Mr. Beese, could you come in the week after the 17th and 18th? That means that the cross-examination of the witness -- and the witness also has other things to attend to, I'm sure, so he will have to consult his calendar, but would that next week be acceptable from the Monday after the week of the 17th? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe that would be appropriate, Your Honour, and of course I do want to stress one point: Mr. Mundis said we have two months to prepare. We need to keep in mind that the 127 pages have not been translated, so it will be less than two months, but I believe that wouldn't be a problem the following week. And since we're only going to have one day, I think it might be best to not even -- you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes. Right. Mr. Beese, you were able to follow the debate. The week -- the 15th of August, I think, is a Tuesday. So that will be Monday the 21st of August. Yes, Monday, the 21st of August at 14.15 hours we would start your cross-examination. And as you have gathered yourself, I'm sure it will take several days. So try and secure that week between the 21st and the 26th of August and place yourself at the disposal of the Trial Chamber. I hope that that will be possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's fine. There we have it. We meet again, Mr. Beese, on the 21st of August at 14.15 hours. I shall now ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom. I wish you a pleasant journey back, and happy holidays.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have a quarter of an hour. Would any of the parties like to make any further suggestions, raise any questions? I can see Mr. Karnavas jumping up, and Counsel Kovacic as well. Let's hear Mr. Karnavas first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe we probably have the same concern. It was brought to my attention during the break, as one of my team members was preparing for the documents for next week, that many of the documents, as I understand, for the next witness are in Spanish and they have yet to be translated into English. That's what I was told. I brought it up to Mr. Mundis's attention, although I don't know whether that's his witness or not. Perhaps we can hear from the Prosecution whether they intend to be introducing Spanish documents or going through the documents with the Spanish-speaking witness, but perhaps we could get some clarification on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll make some inquiries about this following the rising of the Court this afternoon. My understanding from Ms. Winner is that some additional material was placed on EDS as of yesterday. We're in the process of providing the letter and indexes to that. Some of the translations may be in that disclosure. But we'll make these inquiries and inform the Defence later this afternoon as to the status of any outstanding translations concerning the Spanish documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I appreciate that. I would, however, request - and I think it's a minor request, not terribly inconvenient for the Prosecution - to sort of give us the heads-up in advance and let us know these sort of things, because we're basically drowning on this side. I don't know about that side, but we're drowning here. We're barely being able to prepare witness for witness. So if we have some advance notice when they put stuff on the EDS. If they're translating at the last moment, we need to know, because now we spend the entire weekend preparing, and it makes for a very long trial. I mean -- and I understand, Your Honours, you do the same thing, but in any event we do need some advance notice. And as you can see we are trying to be very, very reasonable on this side. I can say the same thing more or less by the Prosecutor, but not always, but more or less. Anyway ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That is the least of it. Mr. Karnavas has raised a problem, Mr. Mundis. As far as I understand it, they are additional documents that probably arrived in the course of the proceedings that you have placed on the electronic system, the EDS, and what you placed on the EDS system were documents in Spanish and thence the difficulty for the Defence, and quite legitimately they would like to have the translations provided as soon as possible. Of course I personally also join in what the Defence has said, and I know that their job is a difficult one in view of the masses and masses of documents that they have to get through and that we hold sittings one day after another with new witnesses coming in and so on. So it's quite considerable work that they have to get through. And if they have additional work because of additional difficulties and new documents, then the Defence is kindly requesting that you could let them know in advance if any documents like that are going to come up, because if they come up on the EDS and they aren't able to confirm and verify them, then either by professional courtesy could you pick up the phone and tell them straight away and tell them that, well, there are five or six new documents that have arrived. I think that is the least you could do in order to help out the Defence counsel with that particular problem. So these fraternal relations will, I hope, prevail and enable justice to march forward. So is that something that you can do? Is it possible? Can you ring up your learned friends and say that's the situation, "We've got new documents coming"? And also to inform the legal officer of the Chamber as well, of course, because I've just discovered this at this late hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think that's something that we can probably accommodate the Defence with, but I do again want to make a point -- I believe a point in this respect, and that is we're not talking about new documents, we're talking about translations of existing documents. And in this instance, because the original documents are in Spanish, I understand that that's different from a situation where the original document is in Bosnian or Croatian or Serbian. But the point is we're not talking about new documents. At least, that's my understanding sitting here today. We're talking about translations of existing documents. And I understand it's a fine line where we're talking about a language that perhaps not as many people in this courtroom can read, but these are not new documents, they are simply translations of documents that are already on the witness list and the original language of which is Spanish. But we will endeavour to communicate to the Defence as soon as additional translations are put into the EDS system for them. And also, if Your Honour wishes, we will convey that to the Chamber's legal officers as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Kovacic, did you want to address the same matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I was going to raise the same subject, but it is already settled. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As far as next week is concerned, Mr. Mundis, could you tell us who the witness is, the number of documents, things like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask to go into private session in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Fine. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meeting is adjourned for today. We reconvene on Monday at 14.15. Have a good weekend, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
